cases.question: Why is the delay for the high exhaust gas temperature alarm 10 s and not 5 s?
retrieved: alarm-philosophy / Exhaust gas temperature delay p.2 cos=0.889
alarm-philosophy / Delay times p.2 cos=0.814
cause-and-effect / Main engine protection p.1 cos=0.807
alarm-philosophy / Priorities and alarm groups p.1 cos=0.762
alarm-philosophy / Purpose and principles p.1 cos=0.752
alarm-philosophy / Limit levels and hysteresis p.1 cos=0.716
cited: alarm-philosophy / Exhaust gas temperature delay p.2
cases.answer: The delay is 10 s and not 5 s for three reasons. First, thermocouple lag: sheathed Type K thermocouples in a thermowell have a time constant of about 4 to 6 s, so a 5 s delay filters almost nothing and starts on a reading that is still moving, whereas 10 s is long enough to confirm the temperature is above the limit and ignore short excursions [alarm-philosophy §Exhaust gas temperature delay p.2]. Second, nuisance alarms during load changes: engine load changes over 10 % within a minute cause exhaust temperatures to overshoot by 10 to 15 degrees C for roughly 5 to 8 s, and a 5 s delay produced 14 nuisance H alarms during manoeuvring compared to none with 10 s [alarm-philosophy §Exhaust gas temperature delay p.2]. Third, the extra wait costs no protection because damage develops over minutes and the real protection is the HH limit with a 2 s delay [alarm-philosophy §Exhaust gas temperature delay p.2].
